question.prompt:
In an equiangular hexagon, all interior angles measure \(120^\circ.\) An example of such a hexagon with side lengths of \(2,\) \(3,\) \(1,\) \(3,\) \(2,\) and \(2\) is shown below, inscribed in equilateral triangle \(ABC.\) Consider all equiangular hexagons with positive integer side lengths that can be inscribed in \(\triangle ABC,\) with all six vertices on the sides of the triangle. What is the total number of such hexagons? Hexagons that differ only by a rotation or a reflection are considered the same.

[Figure 1](figures/2026_AMC_8_Q25_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
Describe each hexagon by the three small triangles cut away from the corners of \(ABC\). This reduces six side lengths to three numbers.

[Figure 1](figures/2026_AMC_8_Q25_question_fig1.svg)

First, every valid hexagon must have exactly two vertices on each side of \(ABC\). A hexagon vertex cannot be at \(A\), \(B\), or \(C\), because a \(120^\circ\) angle cannot fit inside a \(60^\circ\) triangle corner. Also, three hexagon vertices on one straight side would give the middle vertex an angle of \(180^\circ\). With six vertices on three sides, there must therefore be two on each side.

Each removed corner triangle has a \(60^\circ\) angle at the triangle corner. Its other two angles supplement the hexagon's \(120^\circ\) angles, so they are also \(60^\circ\). Thus all three corner triangles are equilateral. In the displayed example, the bottom side of \(ABC\) consequently has length
\[
1+3+2=6.
\]

Let \(a,b,c\) be the side lengths of the equilateral triangles removed at the three corners. They are positive integers because their bases are hexagon sides. The other three hexagon sides have lengths
\[
6-a-b,\qquad 6-b-c,\qquad 6-c-a.
\]
They must all be positive. Conversely, positive integer cuts satisfying these conditions leave a six-sided figure with all interior angles \(120^\circ\), so these conditions describe every valid case.

A rotation can choose which corner comes first, and a reflection can interchange the other two corners. We may therefore list the cuts in sorted order,
\[
1\le a\le b\le c.
\]
The largest pair sum is \(b+c\), so all three remaining sides are positive exactly when \(b+c\le5\). Equality is allowed and leaves a side of length \(1\).

If \(b=1\), then \(a=1\) and \(c\) can be \(1,2,3,4\). This gives
\[
(1,1,1),\ (1,1,2),\ (1,1,3),\ (1,1,4).
\]
If \(b=2\), then \(a\) can be \(1\) or \(2\), and \(c\) can be \(2\) or \(3\). This gives
\[
(1,2,2),\ (1,2,3),\ (2,2,2),\ (2,2,3).
\]
No \(b\ge3\) is possible, because then \(b+c\ge6\). These cases exhaust the possibilities.

We also check that different listed triples do not accidentally give the same hexagon shape. The perimeter is \(18-(a+b+c)\), so triples with different sums give different perimeters. The only repeated sums are \(5\) and \(6\). For sum \(5\), the triples \((1,1,3)\) and \((1,2,2)\) have longest sides \(4\) and \(3\), respectively. For sum \(6\), the triples \((1,1,4)\), \((1,2,3)\), and \((2,2,2)\) have longest sides \(4,3,2\), respectively. Rotations and reflections preserve both perimeter and longest side, so all eight shapes are distinct.

The total is \(4+2\cdot2=\boxed{8}\), choice \(\text{E}\).
solutions.title: Count the three corner cuts
